questions.question: Why does dropout help prevent overfitting?
options: It prevents neurons from co-adapting too much and forces the network to learn more robust, redundant features.
It permanently removes neurons, making the network smaller.
It increases the learning rate.
It adds noise to the labels.
questions.explanation: Dropout prevents co-adaptation by randomly deactivating neurons, forcing the network to learn robust and redundant features.

questions.question: L2 regularization is also known as:
options: Weight decay or Ridge regularization
Lasso regularization
Dropout regularization
Early stopping
questions.explanation: L2 regularization is also called Weight Decay or Ridge Regression, penalizing large weights by adding squared sum to the loss.

questions.question: What is a typical dropout rate mentioned in the material (e.g., probability of dropping a neuron)?
questions.explanation: A dropout rate of 50% (p=0.5) is commonly recommended for hidden layers as a good balance.

questions.question: Which regularization technique reduces model complexity by shrinking weights but typically does not set them to zero?
options: L2 regularization (Ridge)
L1 regularization (Lasso)
Dropout
Data augmentation
questions.explanation: L2 regularization shrinks weights toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero, unlike L1 which drives some weights to zero.

questions.question: Which metric is commonly monitored to decide when to apply early stopping?
options: Validation loss (or another chosen metric) at the end of every epoch.
Training accuracy at the beginning of each epoch.
Number of parameters in the model.
The learning rate value.
questions.explanation: Validation loss is commonly monitored for early stopping as it indicates generalization performance.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of regularization?
options: To improve generalization of the model on unseen data by preventing overfitting.
To achieve zero training loss at all costs.
To increase the model's variance.
To make the model more complex and capture noise.
questions.explanation: Regularization aims to improve generalization by preventing overfitting, even if it slightly increases training error.

questions.question: What is underfitting in the context of model fitting?
options: The model is not complex enough to explain the data well, resulting in poor predictive performance.
The model is too complex and describes noise instead of the underlying relationship.
The model perfectly memorizes the training data but fails on new data.
The model has high variance and low bias.
questions.explanation: Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern, resulting in poor predictive performance.

questions.question: Which of the following are examples of data augmentation for image classification mentioned in the material?
options: Translation, rotation, scaling, or deformation of images.
Adding random noise to labels.
Removing all color channels.
Doubling the image resolution.
questions.explanation: Common image augmentations include translation, rotation, scaling, flipping, and deformation.

questions.question: What does L2 regularization prefer in terms of weight distribution?
options: It prefers to 'spread out' the weights (lower sum of squares).
It prefers many weights to be exactly zero.
It prefers one weight to be very large and others zero.
It has no preference on weight distribution.
questions.explanation: L2 regularization spreads weights evenly with smaller magnitudes because it penalizes the sum of squared weights.

questions.question: Why is L1 regularization useful for feature selection?
options: It nullifies the contribution of less important features by setting their weights to zero, leading to a sparse model.
It spreads weights evenly across all features.
It increases all weights to the same value.
It removes features with high variance.
questions.explanation: L1 regularization drives weights to zero, effectively performing feature selection by removing less important features.

questions.question: What is regularization in machine learning?
options: A technique that constrains the optimization problem to discourage complex models, limiting the capacity of a model to avoid overfitting.
A method to increase model complexity to better fit training data.
A process of adding more layers to a neural network.
A way to increase the learning rate during training.
questions.explanation: Regularization adds constraints that penalize complexity, encouraging simpler models that generalize better.

questions.question: According to the material, regularization works by either:
options: Adding a penalty to the loss function or modifying the network's architecture during training.
Increasing the number of epochs or decreasing the batch size.
Using a larger learning rate or more training data.
Removing all bias terms or increasing the number of layers.
questions.explanation: Regularization can be applied as a penalty term in the loss function (e.g., L1/L2) or through architectural modifications (e.g., Dropout).

questions.question: Which statement best describes the performance of an underfitted model?
options: Poor predictive performance due to the model not being complex enough to explain the data.
Excellent performance on training data but poor on test data.
Perfect generalization to unseen data.
High variance and low bias.
questions.explanation: Underfitting results in poor predictive performance because the model is too simple to capture the underlying data patterns.

questions.question: Which regularization technique encourages many weights to become exactly zero, leading to a sparse model?
options: L1 regularization (Lasso)
L2 regularization (Ridge)
Dropout
Early stopping
questions.explanation: L1 regularization (Lasso) drives weights to exactly zero, making it useful for feature selection and sparse models.

questions.question: The regularization strength λ (lambda) is a:
options: Hyperparameter that must be tuned.
Parameter learned during training.
Fixed constant always set to 1.
Derivative of the loss function.
questions.explanation: λ controls the strength of regularization and is a hyperparameter that must be tuned for optimal performance.

questions.question: What is the penalty term added to the loss function for L2 (Ridge) regularization?
options: λ ∑ w_i²
λ ∑ |w_i|
λ ∑ w_i
questions.explanation: L2 penalty is the sum of squared weights (Σ w_i²) multiplied by the regularization strength λ.

questions.question: In TensorFlow/Keras, which layer is used to implement dropout?
options: tf.keras.layers.Dropout(p=0.5)
tf.keras.layers.Regularizer()
tf.keras.layers.L1()
tf.keras.layers.L2()
questions.explanation: Dropout is implemented using tf.keras.layers.Dropout with the probability parameter p.

questions.question: L1 regularization is also known as:
options: Lasso regularization
Ridge regularization
Weight decay
Dropout
questions.explanation: L1 regularization is called Lasso (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) regularization.

questions.question: When is dropout regularization applied?
options: Only during training. The full intact network is used for prediction on validation/test sets.
Only during testing. Training uses the full network.
Both during training and testing with the same dropout rate.
Only during the first epoch.
questions.explanation: Dropout is applied only during training. During inference, all neurons are active and weights are scaled.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of data augmentation as a regularization technique?
options: To create additional synthetic data by perturbing existing training instances, thereby training with more data to improve generalization.
To reduce the number of training samples to speed up training.
To remove noise from the dataset.
To increase model complexity.
questions.explanation: Data augmentation generates new training samples through transformations to improve generalization.
